title: Bayesian Inference
subtitle: Topic: Bayesian Inference · Subject: Bayesian and Probabilistic Modeling · Seven illustrated questions on Bayes’ rule, prevalence and base rates, conjugate Beta updates, credible intervals, runnable posterior sampling, predictive dependence, and prior/model sensitivity.
hero:
BAYESIAN INFERENCE · BAYESIAN AND PROBABILISTIC MODELING

Update what you believe when new evidence arrives

Learn how priors, data likelihoods and evidence produce posteriors—then turn those distributions into credible intervals, predictive probabilities, and defensible decisions.

PriorEvidencePosterior and forecast

The displayed Beta–Bernoulli example assumes conditionally independent successes given a fixed underlying probability. Model and prior assumptions matter.

questions.stem: How does Bayesian inference combine a prior, likelihood, and evidence into a posterior, and why is the normalizing evidence term needed?
options: Bayesian inference treats the prior as a probability of observations and the likelihood as a probability of parameters. It multiplies both to obtain posterior weights, with the evidence measuring only the most likely observed outcome.

Bayesian inference combines prior and likelihood, then divides their product by the likelihood at the best-fitting parameter. This normalizes the posterior by ignoring parameter settings that describe the observations less successfully.

Bayesian inference multiplies the parameter prior by the data likelihood and divides by evidence, the prior-weighted likelihood summed across parameter possibilities. This normalizes the posterior probabilities so that they total one.

Bayesian inference estimates the posterior from the likelihood alone, then uses the prior to assess whether its predictions seem plausible. Evidence is an adjustment applied after fitting rather than a normalizing probability.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Bayesian inference updates beliefs about unknown parameters using observed evidence. The prior expresses plausibility before seeing the data, while the likelihood says how compatible the observed data are with each parameter setting. Multiplying them yields unnormalized posterior weights. Evidence—the likelihood averaged under the prior—makes those weights sum or integrate to one. For example, a factory may start with prior beliefs about a machine's defect rate and update them after inspecting products. The likelihood of the inspection results changes which rates appear plausible.
questions.figure:
01 · VISUAL LESSON

Bayes’ rule balances prior plausibility with how well data fit a hypothesis

p(θ|D) = p(D|θ)p(θ)/p(D)Evidence normalizesLikelihood is not posterior

Bayesian inference updates uncertainty about a hypothesis or parameter θ using data D. A prior assigns plausibility before D; the likelihood measures how compatible D is with each θ. The evidence sums or integrates prior-weighted likelihoods and normalizes the posterior.

questions.tag: Beginner · Bayes’ theorem and base rates
questions.stem: Why can a medical screening test with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity still give only about a 15% probability of a rare condition after a positive result?
options: If the condition affects 1% of 10,000 people, 90 of 100 affected people test positive but 495 unaffected people also test positive. Among 585 positive results, only 90 have the condition, or about 15.4%.

With sensitivity of 90%, 90 of every 100 positive tests must be true positives regardless of prevalence. Specificity only controls how many negative tests are correct and does not enter the posterior probability of disease.
With specificity of 95%, 95% of positive results are correct whenever prevalence is below 5%. The remaining 5% of positives are false, so a positive test raises disease probability to roughly 95%.

Among 10,000 people, 1% prevalence means 100 have the condition and 9,900 do not. After a positive test, the denominator should include all 10,000 people rather than only positive results, giving about 0.9%.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Sensitivity means P(positive|condition), not P(condition|positive). Bayes' rule must also count the large unaffected group and the test's false-positive rate of 5%. With 1% prevalence in 10,000 people, there are about 90 true positives and 495 false positives, for 585 positive results. Only 90/585 ≈ 15.4% are affected. This example is an illustration of base-rate reasoning, not a claim about a particular medical test. Individual decisions require validated prevalence, test performance, and clinical interpretation.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

Rare events can stay uncommon even after a positive test

Before testing1% prevalence means 100 of 10,000 people have the condition in this illustration.
Among positive tests90 true positives and 495 false positives give 90/585 ≈ 15.4%, not 90%.

A test's sensitivity is P(positive|condition), not P(condition|positive). Bayes' rule includes the low base rate and false-positive results among those without the condition. A rare condition can therefore have a modest posterior even after a positive test.

questions.stem: How does a Beta prior update after Bernoulli successes and failures, and why can its posterior mean differ from the maximum-likelihood estimate?
options: A Beta(a,b) prior gains one success count and one failure count for every new observation, giving Beta(a+n,b+n). Its posterior mean equals the observed success fraction because prior counts disappear after updating.

A Beta prior keeps its original shape, while the likelihood changes its mean after every observed success. The posterior distribution is therefore determined by the observed fraction alone, with no contribution from earlier beliefs.

A Beta(a,b) prior updates to Beta(a+failures,b+successes), because failures increase the first parameter. The posterior mean equals the sample failure rate, while the maximum-likelihood estimate uses the sample success fraction.

Beta(a,b) updates to Beta(a+successes,b+failures) for Bernoulli data. Its posterior mean includes prior counts: Beta(2,2) with eight successes and two failures gives 10/14, unlike the sample estimate 8/10.
questions.explanation: Explanation: The Beta distribution is conjugate to Bernoulli or binomial observations: a Beta(a,b) prior becomes Beta(a+s,b+f) after s successes and f failures. Its posterior mean is (a+s)/(a+b+s+f). The maximum-likelihood estimate is s/(s+f), so the two need not match. For example, a wireless sensor succeeds on eight of ten transmissions. Starting with Beta(2,2), the updated distribution is Beta(10,4), with mean 0.714. The observed success fraction alone is 0.8; the prior moderates this estimate.
questions.figure:
03 · VISUAL LESSON

A Beta prior and Bernoulli observations produce another Beta distribution

Prior mean: 0.500Observed fraction: 0.800Posterior mean: 0.714

For conditionally independent Bernoulli outcomes with fixed success probability θ, a Beta(a,b) prior updates to Beta(a+s,b+f) after s successes and f failures. The posterior mean and the maximum-likelihood estimate generally differ when the prior carries information.

questions.tag: Medium · Bayesian credible versus frequentist confidence intervals
questions.stem: What does a 95% Bayesian credible interval mean for an unknown parameter, and how is that interpretation different from a frequentist 95% confidence interval?
options: A 95% credible interval says 95% of future measurements will lie in the reported range, while a 95% confidence interval describes probabilities for the parameter after conditioning on the observed sample.

A 95% credible interval contains 95% posterior probability for a parameter given the data and model. A frequentist 95% confidence procedure covers the fixed parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions.

A 95% Bayesian credible interval means 95% of repeated fitted intervals would cover the unknown parameter, while a frequentist interval assigns 95% posterior probability to the parameter inside one already-computed range.

A 95% credible interval and a 95% confidence interval give identical probability statements if their numerical endpoints match. Both assert the same 95% chance that the fixed parameter lies within the particular realized interval.
questions.explanation: Explanation: In Bayesian inference, a 95% credible interval contains 95% of the posterior probability for the unknown parameter, conditional on the chosen prior, likelihood and data. In frequentist inference, the true parameter is fixed, and a 95% confidence procedure has 95% long-run coverage under repeated sampling. Neither automatically describes the range of a future observation. For example, a researcher may report posterior uncertainty about a building's energy-efficiency parameter. That parameter interval must not be read as predicting 95% of future energy readings.
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

A credible interval describes a posterior parameter distribution; confidence is about a procedure

Posterior probabilityProbability for the unknown parameter is conditioned on the data and Bayesian model.
Repeated samplingThe confidence procedure has a long-run coverage property; the computed endpoints change across datasets.

A 95% Bayesian credible interval contains 95% posterior probability for the parameter, conditional on the prior, model and observed data. A 95% frequentist confidence procedure covers the fixed true parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions. Neither interval automatically describes a future observation.

questions.tag: Medium · Python posterior sampling and prediction
questions.stem: How can a short Python program update a Beta–Bernoulli posterior, approximate a credible interval from posterior samples, and calculate the probability of success on the next trial?
options: Python can draw a Beta prior, update its endpoints using the observed sample fraction, and treat the resulting interval as a range of future Bernoulli outcomes. The next-success probability should equal the observed fraction regardless of the prior.

Python can compute Beta posterior parameters from trial counts, but the credible interval should use repeated sampling of new labels instead of posterior parameter draws. The next-event probability comes from the largest sampled parameter.

Python can fit a Bernoulli maximum-likelihood estimate and create a credible interval by averaging the observed successes and failures. That interval has an automatic frequentist coverage guarantee even without a specified prior distribution.

Python can add successes and failures to the Beta prior parameters, sample that posterior to approximate a parameter credible interval, and use its mean as the next Bernoulli success probability under the shared-rate model.
questions.explanation: Explanation: For a Beta–Bernoulli model, update the prior parameters by adding observed successes and failures. Standard Python can draw Beta-distributed parameter samples; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles approximate a 95% equal-tailed credible interval. The posterior mean predicts the probability of success on the next Bernoulli trial. For example, a subscription experiment with eight sign-ups and two non-sign-ups, starting from Beta(2,2), yields Beta(10,4). The seeded example prints probability 0.714 and an approximate credible interval [0.462, 0.910] for the unknown sign-up rate.
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Python computes a posterior, draws plausible rates, and predicts the next trial

Python · Beta–Bernoulli posterior and credible interval 12 lines · standard library · CPU-tested
import random
random.seed(7)
successes, failures = 8, 2
prior_a, prior_b = 2, 2
post_a, post_b = prior_a + successes, prior_b + failures
draws = sorted(random.betavariate(post_a, post_b) for _ in range(20000))
low = draws[int(.025 * len(draws))]
high = draws[int(.975 * len(draws))]
next_success = post_a / (post_a + post_b)
print('posterior:', (post_a, post_b))
print('next success:', round(next_success, 3))
print('95% credible approx:', (round(low, 3), round(high, 3)))
Verified output: posterior: (10, 4); next success: 0.714; 95% credible approx: (0.462, 0.91). The equal-tailed interval is a seeded Monte Carlo approximation for θ, not an interval for one future binary outcome. The model assumes Bernoulli trials share a fixed unknown success probability.

Beta–Bernoulli conjugacy makes this example runnable with standard Python. Posterior samples approximate uncertainty about the unknown success rate. For a single next Bernoulli trial, the posterior predictive success probability equals the posterior mean.

questions.stem: How does Bayesian posterior predictive inference calculate the probability of two future successes, and why can that differ from squaring the single-trial posterior predictive mean?
options: Two future Bernoulli trials have marginal success probability 10/14 each, so the probability both succeed is always (10/14)². Integrating over the posterior leaves them independent because the parameter is the same for both trials.

Two future trials share a hidden success rate, but the posterior predictive calculation should multiply their likelihoods using the most probable parameter value. The posterior mean must be replaced by the maximum-likelihood fraction 8/10.

With Beta(10,4), the first success has probability 10/14 and updates the posterior to Beta(11,4). The second succeeds with probability 11/15, making both successes 0.524 after integrating out the parameter.

Two future successes require two posterior updates before either event is observed, so both use success probability 11/15. The joint probability therefore equals (11/15)², not the posterior predictive probability for one trial squared.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Posterior predictive inference averages over uncertain parameter values. Future Bernoulli trials are independent conditional on the shared success rate θ, but become dependent after θ is integrated out. Under Beta(10,4), the next success probability is 10/14. If that trial succeeds, the posterior becomes Beta(11,4), so the next success probability is 11/15. The joint probability is (10/14)×(11/15) ≈ 0.524, slightly above (10/14)² ≈ 0.510. For example, two upcoming product quality checks share the same uncertain process reliability.
questions.figure:
06 · VISUAL LESSON

Two future observations share uncertainty about the same hidden success rate

P(first success): 10/14P(second success | first): 11/15P(both): 0.524

Posterior predictive inference averages future-data probabilities over the posterior, not merely over one fitted rate. Multiple future Bernoulli outcomes are independent given θ but generally dependent after θ is integrated out. The first result changes the predictive probability for the second.

questions.tag: Advanced · Prior sensitivity and posterior predictive checks
questions.stem: Why can strong priors and incorrect likelihood assumptions distort Bayesian posterior conclusions, and how can sensitivity analysis and posterior predictive checks reveal weaknesses before decisions?
options: With sparse data, strong priors can substantially alter posteriors, while wrong likelihood assumptions can distort conclusions. Compare plausible priors and simulated predictive outcomes with observations, then validate forecasts on new conditions.

Strong priors influence the posterior only before any observations arrive; after a single measured event the likelihood determines everything. Posterior predictive checks certify a model whenever average simulated values match the sample mean.

Strong priors prevent model misspecification by constraining predictions toward known values. Sensitivity analysis therefore changes only the numerical optimization settings, while predictive checks measure convergence speed rather than fit to real data.

Bayesian updating ensures a posterior is reliable even if the sample is selected unfairly or the likelihood omits key mechanisms. Posterior predictive checks are useful only to confirm that the prior distribution has enough probability mass.
questions.explanation: Explanation: When data are sparse, different defensible priors can yield noticeably different posteriors. Likelihood errors or biased samples can also produce misleading certainty. Sensitivity analysis repeats inference with alternative priors; posterior predictive checks generate replicated data from the fitted model and compare meaningful features with observations. For example, after three successes and two failures, Beta(1,1) gives posterior mean 4/7≈0.571, while an optimistic Beta(20,2) yields 23/27≈0.852. A new-market launch should check whether these beliefs and forecasts withstand additional evidence and deployment changes.
questions.figure:
07 · VISUAL LESSON

A strong prior can dominate sparse data; model checks test more than posterior fit

Prior sensitivityCheck which conclusions change when plausible prior assumptions vary.
Posterior predictive checkSimulate data using the fitted model and compare key patterns with actual data.
Deployment robustnessTest held-out populations, selection bias and the consequences of confident mistakes.

Sparse data may leave substantial prior influence. A prior-sensitivity analysis repeats inference under defensible priors; posterior predictive checks compare replicated outcomes with observed patterns. Neither protects automatically against biased sampling, wrong likelihoods, or deployment shift.
